title: Disabling Interrupts Isn't a Lock
prompt: On an old single-core machine, an OS could protect a critical section just by disabling interrupts. Why doesn't that work on a multicore CPU, and what do real locks use instead?
key_points: On one core, the only way another thread can interleave is a context switch, which needs an interrupt (e.g. the timer); with interrupts disabled, the critical section runs uninterrupted.
On multicore, disabling interrupts only affects the current core; threads on other cores keep running and can access the same memory at the same time.
Real locks rely on atomic hardware instructions (test-and-set, compare-and-swap, `LOCK`-prefixed ops, LL/SC) that the cache-coherence protocol makes atomic across cores.

Disabling interrupts is also privileged (user code can't do it) and dangerous (lost interrupts, a buggy section hangs the machine), so even kernels use it only for very short sections, together with spinlocks.
model_answer:
Mutual exclusion means no other thread can run the critical section at the same time. On a single core, the only way the current thread can be paused and another one run is via an interrupt: the timer fires and the scheduler preempts. Disable interrupts, and nothing can preempt you until you re-enable them.

On a multicore machine, the other threads aren't waiting to be scheduled on *your* core; they're already running on other cores. Disabling interrupts on core 0 doesn't stop core 1 from executing the same critical section on the same data.

So locks are built on **atomic read-modify-write instructions**: test-and-set, compare-and-swap (`lock cmpxchg` on x86), or load-linked/store-conditional on ARM/RISC-V. The cache-coherence protocol guarantees that only one core's atomic operation on a cache line succeeds at a time. A spinlock loops on CAS, and a mutex spins briefly and then asks the kernel to sleep (futex on Linux).

Kernels still disable interrupts *locally* in combination with spinlocks, so that an interrupt handler on the same core doesn't deadlock trying to take a lock the interrupted code already holds. Interrupts alone are never enough on SMP.
